# Introduction

The main research question of our group project is:

**How well can we classify Premier League match outcomes using models trained on lower English football leagues?**

For my part of the project, I developed two Random Forest models to investigate this question.

The first model uses 12 full-time match statistics, while the second model includes three additional Bet365 betting odds features.

Both models classify match outcomes into three categories:

- **H:** Home win
- **D:** Draw
- **A:** Away win

Random Forest was selected because it combines multiple decision trees and can capture complex relationships between football match statistics and results.

The main aim is to examine whether patterns learned from lower-league football matches can also be applied to Premier League matches. I also investigate whether including betting odds improves classification performance.

# Dataset

## Data Source

The dataset contains historical English football match data obtained from Football-Data.co.uk.

The data was processed by a group member and divided according to the football league.

The training dataset includes matches from:

- Championship (E1)
- League One (E2)
- League Two (E3)

The test dataset includes matches from:

- Premier League (E0)

| Dataset | Leagues | Number of Matches |
|---|---|---:|
| Training | Championship, League One, League Two | 37,824 |
| Testing | Premier League | 8,740 |
| Total | Four English leagues | 46,564 |

The processed datasets were stored in:

- `processed-data/football_train_data.csv`
- `processed-data/football_test_data.csv`

The models were trained on lower-league data and evaluated on Premier League data. This allows us to investigate how well a model generalises across different English football divisions.

## Selected Features

The baseline Random Forest used 12 numerical features representing full-time match statistics.

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| HS | Home team shots |
| AS | Away team shots |
| HST | Home team shots on target |
| AST | Away team shots on target |
| HF | Home team fouls |
| AF | Away team fouls |
| HC | Home team corners |
| AC | Away team corners |
| HY | Home team yellow cards |
| AY | Away team yellow cards |
| HR | Home team red cards |
| AR | Away team red cards |

Full-time goals (`FTHG` and `FTAG`) were excluded because they directly determine the match result. Including them would cause direct target leakage.

## Additional Betting Odds Features

The second model uses the same 12 statistics together with three Bet365 betting odds features.

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| B365H | Bet365 home win odds |
| B365D | Bet365 draw odds |
| B365A | Bet365 away win odds |

The model with odds therefore contains 15 predictors.

The purpose of adding these features is to investigate whether betting market information improves the classification of match outcomes.

# Exploratory Data Analysis

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) was conducted to understand relationships between match statistics and outcomes.

The analysis included:

- Shots on target
- Differences in home and away shots
- Corner differences
- Home-versus-away attacking performance

These visualisations helped us explore which match statistics might be useful for classification.

Shots on target appeared to be particularly relevant, supporting their inclusion in the Random Forest model.

# Missing Data Analysis

## Identifying Missing Values

Before training the baseline Random Forest, the selected 12 numerical predictors were checked for missing values.

There were 16 missing feature values distributed across three training observations.

The home and away foul variables each contained three missing values. Each of the other ten predictors contained one missing value.

No missing values were identified in these selected predictors in the test dataset.

Because the number of affected observations was small, different missing-data handling methods were compared.

## Missing Data Handling Methods

Five approaches were considered.

### Complete-case Analysis

Complete-case analysis removes observations containing missing values in the required predictors.

In this project, three training observations were removed from the baseline model.

This method is simple and avoids estimating missing values. However, deleting incomplete observations may introduce bias if missingness is systematic.

### Available-case Analysis

Available-case analysis uses all available observations for each statistical calculation.

In this project, it was used for descriptive statistics and correlation analysis rather than as a separate Random Forest training method.

### Mean Imputation

Mean imputation replaces missing numerical values with the mean of the corresponding feature.

This method preserves sample size but may underestimate variability.

### Regression Imputation

Regression imputation estimates missing values using relationships between the incomplete feature and other observed predictors.

Its performance depends on the regression assumptions and the quality of the estimated relationships.

### Multiple Imputation

Multiple imputation creates several plausible completed datasets to reflect uncertainty in missing values.

In this project, five imputed datasets were generated, and the resulting Random Forest predictions were combined.

This approach is more computationally demanding but provides a way to reflect uncertainty related to missing observations.

## Comparison of Missing Data Methods

Four methods were compared through Random Forest classification. Available-case analysis was used separately for descriptive analysis.

| Method | Accuracy | Macro F1 | Draw Recall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Complete-case Analysis | 57.21% | 45.76% | 6.21% |
| Mean Imputation | 56.97% | 45.57% | 6.25% |
| Regression Imputation | 56.99% | 45.54% | 6.07% |
| Multiple Imputation | 57.16% | 45.61% | 5.93% |

Complete-case analysis achieved the highest overall accuracy and Macro F1-score.

However, the differences were small. The highest and lowest accuracy values differed by only 0.24 percentage points.

Because only three training observations contained missing values in the selected predictors, complete-case analysis was selected for the baseline Random Forest model.

This does not mean complete-case analysis is always better than imputation. It was an appropriate choice for this particular dataset and model configuration.

## Missing Values in the Odds Model

The model with odds required all 15 selected predictors.

After applying complete-case analysis, 12 training observations were removed.

| Dataset | Baseline RF | RF with Odds |
|---|---:|---:|
| Original training observations | 37,824 | 37,824 |
| Removed observations | 3 | 12 |
| Remaining training observations | 37,821 | 37,812 |
| Test observations | 8,740 | 8,740 |

The number of removed observations remained small compared with the full training dataset.

# Random Forest Model Implementation

## Model Configuration

Both models were implemented using Python and scikit-learn.

The same hyperparameters were used in both experiments.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Model | RandomForestClassifier |
| Number of trees | 200 |
| Maximum tree depth | 12 |
| Random state | 42 |
| Parallel processing | -1 |

The following Python code shows the main model configuration.

```{python rf-baseline, eval=FALSE}
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

model = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=200,
    max_depth=12,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Train on complete lower-league observations
model.fit(X_train_clean, y_train_clean)

# Classify Premier League test matches
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

# Predict class probabilities
y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)
```

The complete executable implementation is available in:

`BingquanW/04_RandomForest/RandomForest.ipynb`

## Random Forest with Betting Odds

The second Random Forest used 15 predictors, including B365H, B365D and B365A.

It used the same model settings as the baseline, allowing the effect of adding odds to be examined.

After complete-case analysis, 37,812 training observations remained.

The complete executable implementation is available in:

`BingquanW/05_RandomForest_WithOdds/RandomForest_WithOdds.ipynb`

## Evaluation Metrics

The models were evaluated using the following metrics:

**Accuracy** measures the proportion of correctly classified matches.

**Macro F1-score** gives equal weight to home wins, draws and away wins.

**Draw Recall** measures how many actual drawn matches were correctly identified.

**Multiclass ROC-AUC** evaluates the ability of the model to distinguish between the three outcomes using predicted probabilities. The One-vs-Rest approach with macro averaging was used.

**Multiclass Log Loss** measures the quality of predicted class probabilities. Lower values indicate better probabilistic predictions.

**AIC** is not reported because standard Akaike Information Criterion is not directly applicable to Random Forest, which does not have a conventional likelihood-based formulation and clearly defined number of estimated parameters.

The following code shows the additional probability-based evaluation.

```{python rf-probability-metrics, eval=FALSE}
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    roc_auc_score,
    log_loss
)

accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)

auc = roc_auc_score(
    y_test,
    y_proba,
    labels=model.classes_,
    multi_class="ovr",
    average="macro"
)

loss = log_loss(
    y_test,
    y_proba,
    labels=model.classes_
)

print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")
print(f"Multiclass ROC-AUC: {auc:.4f}")
print(f"Multiclass Log Loss: {loss:.4f}")
```

# Results and Model Comparison

## Overall Performance

Both Random Forest models were evaluated using Premier League match data.

| Metric | Random Forest | Random Forest with Odds |
|---|---:|---:|
| Accuracy | 57.21% | **59.61%** |
| Macro F1-score | 45.76% | **47.41%** |
| Draw Recall | **6.21%** | 5.14% |
| Multiclass ROC-AUC | 0.7134 | **0.7419** |
| Multiclass Log Loss | 0.9240 | **0.8839** |
| AIC | N/A | N/A |

The Random Forest with betting odds performed better on the main overall evaluation metrics.

## Accuracy Comparison

The baseline Random Forest achieved an accuracy of 57.21%.

After adding betting odds, accuracy increased to 59.61%, an improvement of 2.40 percentage points.

This suggests that betting odds provide additional information that helps the model classify Premier League match outcomes.

## Multiclass ROC-AUC

The baseline Random Forest achieved a multiclass ROC-AUC of 0.7134.

The model with betting odds achieved 0.7419.

The improvement of 0.0285 suggests that the odds-enhanced model had better overall discrimination between home wins, draws and away wins.

## Multiclass Log Loss

The baseline model achieved a multiclass log loss of 0.9240.

The model with odds achieved 0.8839.

Since lower log loss is better, the odds-enhanced model produced better probability predictions on the Premier League test dataset.

Log loss also provides a useful metric for the group's comparison between Random Forest and XGBoost, provided the outcome labels and evaluation data are consistent.

## Draw Classification

Although betting odds improved overall performance, draw classification remained a major weakness.

Draw recall decreased from 6.21% in the baseline model to 5.14% in the model with odds.

This shows that better overall accuracy does not necessarily mean better performance for every outcome category.

## Confusion Matrices

Confusion matrices were used to compare predicted and actual match outcomes.

The baseline model performed better at identifying home wins than draws.

Many drawn matches were incorrectly classified as home wins or away wins.

The odds-enhanced model also struggled to classify draws accurately.

The saved figures are:

- `rf_complete_case_confusion_matrix.png`
- `rf_with_odds_confusion_matrix.png`

# Feature Importance

## Baseline Random Forest

Random Forest feature importance was examined to investigate which statistics contributed most strongly to the model's classifications.

The five most important predictors were approximately:

| Feature | Importance |
|---|---:|
| Home shots on target (HST) | 22.45% |
| Away shots on target (AST) | 19.97% |
| Home corners (HC) | 8.10% |
| Home shots (HS) | 8.03% |
| Away shots (AS) | 7.68% |

Home and away shots on target were the two most influential predictors.

This suggests that attacking performance was strongly associated with how the model classified match outcomes.

## Random Forest with Odds

The model with betting odds included the same match statistics and three additional odds variables.

The betting odds contributed additional information about the relative likelihood of the three possible outcomes.

The improvement in Accuracy, ROC-AUC and Log Loss suggests that adding these features was useful for the overall classification task.

However, Random Forest feature importance should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal relationship.

# Limitations

## Difficulty Predicting Draws

Both Random Forest models performed poorly when identifying draws.

Draw recall remained below 7%, even after adding betting odds.

Future improvements could investigate class imbalance, class weighting and alternative feature engineering.

## Missing Data Assumptions

Complete-case analysis removes observations containing missing values.

Although the number of removed training observations was small, the approach may introduce bias if missingness is related to the characteristics of the matches.

The comparison of missing-data methods was carried out for the baseline model, but not all methods were repeated for the odds-enhanced model.

## Full-Time Statistics and Data Availability

Both models used full-time match statistics such as shots, fouls, corners and cards.

These values are only fully available after a match has finished.

Therefore, the models should be interpreted as **retrospective classification models rather than genuine pre-match forecasting models**.

Although betting odds may be available before kick-off, the odds-enhanced model still uses full-time match statistics.

A genuine pre-match forecasting model would require features available before the match begins.

## Model Configuration

Both models used fixed hyperparameters rather than an extensive optimisation procedure.

Future work could investigate stratified k-fold cross-validation and different Random Forest configurations, including tree depth, minimum leaf size and class weights.

Hyperparameter selection should be performed using training data, with the Premier League test dataset reserved for final evaluation.

## Cross-League Generalisation

The models were trained on Championship, League One and League Two matches but evaluated on Premier League matches.

Football statistics and playing styles may differ across leagues.

Therefore, relationships learned from lower-league matches may not transfer perfectly to the Premier League.

The reported performance shows how the models classified the available Premier League test matches, but it does not guarantee the same performance in different seasons or future datasets.

## Comparison with Other Models

The group developed different machine learning approaches, including XGBoost and other classifiers.

Using consistent metrics such as Accuracy, ROC-AUC and Multiclass Log Loss can help compare their performance.

However, models should be evaluated on comparable test data, and differences in available features should be considered when interpreting results.

# Conclusion

This project investigated how well Random Forest models trained on lower English football leagues could classify Premier League match outcomes.

The models were trained using Championship, League One and League Two match data and evaluated using Premier League matches.

Two versions were developed: a baseline Random Forest using 12 full-time match statistics and a second model including three additional Bet365 betting odds features.

Five missing-data handling approaches were considered. Four were compared through Random Forest classification, while available-case analysis was used for descriptive analysis.

Complete-case analysis was selected for the baseline model because it achieved slightly better overall accuracy and Macro F1-score while removing only three training observations.

The baseline Random Forest achieved an accuracy of **57.21%**, a multiclass ROC-AUC of **0.7134** and a multiclass log loss of **0.9240**.

After adding betting odds, accuracy improved to **59.61%**, ROC-AUC increased to **0.7419**, and log loss decreased to **0.8839**. Macro F1-score also increased from 45.76% to 47.41%.

These results suggest that Random Forest can identify useful relationships between full-time match statistics and results across English football leagues. Betting odds also provided additional information that improved overall classification performance.

However, both models performed poorly when predicting the draw category. This demonstrates that improved overall performance does not necessarily mean improved classification for every class.

Another important limitation is that the models use full-time statistics. Therefore, the results demonstrate retrospective match-outcome classification rather than genuine pre-match forecasting.

Overall, **the Random Forest model with betting odds achieved better performance on the Premier League test dataset across the main overall evaluation metrics**.

Future improvements could include handling class imbalance, optimising model parameters using cross-validation, and developing a separate model using only pre-match information.

These results also provide a basis for comparison with other group models, particularly XGBoost, using consistent evaluation metrics.
